batchName: Late Republic: Caesar in Gaul (58-50 BCE) - Latin words
chapterName: Late Republic: Caesar in Gaul (58-50 BCE)
description: Written by hand from the chapter text: the Latin words it explains

questions.question: Alesia was an oppidum. What is that?
options: A sacred grove of the druids
questions.explanation: It almost certainly stood on Mont Auxois, in eastern France.
questions.sourceQuote: a hilltop fortified town (*oppidum*) of the Mandubii tribe.

questions.question: Who leapt into the sea first when Caesar landed in Britain?
options: The signifer, the standard bearer of the Tenth Legion
A centurion of the Seventh Legion
questions.explanation: The soldiers followed rather than lose their standard.
questions.sourceQuote: the standard bearer (*signifer*) of the Tenth Legion leapt into the sea

questions.question: What did the Senate refuse Caesar after Gaul, for political reasons?
options: A triumphus, the parade that crowned a career
questions.explanation: It did decree 20 days of thanksgiving for Alesia.
questions.sourceQuote: it refused him a triumph (*triumphus*), the parade that crowned a general's career.

questions.question: In 58 BC the Helvetii gave Caesar a casus belli. What is that?
questions.explanation: Historians agree he wanted the war mainly for plunder and glory.
questions.sourceQuote: handed him the justification for war (*casus belli*) he needed.

questions.question: What were the impedimenta of a legion?
options: Its baggage train of about a thousand pack animals
questions.explanation: The train stretched some 4 km (2.5 miles) on the march, and hunger often dictated Caesar’s moves.
questions.sourceQuote: its baggage train (*impedimenta*), which stretched some 4 km (2.5 miles) on the march.

questions.question: Into how many cohortes was a legion of Caesar’s time split?
questions.explanation: The cohort had replaced the smaller maniple.
questions.sourceQuote: Each legion was split into ten cohorts (*cohortes*) of 480 soldiers.

questions.question: In 44 BC Caesar was named dictator perpetuus. What does it mean?
questions.explanation: He had crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC and won the civil war that followed.
questions.sourceQuote: In 44 BC he was named dictator for life (*dictator perpetuus*).

questions.question: What were Caesar’s Commentarii de Bello Gallico?
options: His own account of the war, sent to Rome in instalments
The Senate’s records of the war
A Gallic history of the war
questions.explanation: The Gauls wrote no histories, so almost everything known about the war comes from Caesar.
questions.sourceQuote: His Commentaries on the Gallic War (*Commentarii de Bello Gallico*) reached Rome in instalments
